domain: Transportation Systems / Coordination Economics / Institutional Path Dependence
topic_summary: Analysis of the convention of driving on the right-hand side of the road as a coordination mechanism. The topic examines why approximately 65% of the world's population drives on the right, the historical origins of this convention, and the structural forces that maintain it despite the existence of a viable alternative (left-hand driving).

key_entities: Right-hand traffic convention (coordination norm adopted by ~165 countries)
Left-hand traffic convention (coordination norm adopted by ~75 countries, including UK, Japan, India)
National transportation authorities (enforcement and standardization bodies)
Vehicle manufacturers (design constraints based on market conventions)
Border regions (zones where conventions collide physically)
key_tensions: Network effects vs switching costs (benefits of global standardization vs cost of transition)
Historical path dependence vs rational optimization (inherited convention vs theoretically optimal choice)
key_mechanisms: Legal enforcement (traffic laws mandate side; violations penalized)
Infrastructure lock-in (road design, signage, vehicle manufacturing tooled to convention)
Coordination cascade (once critical mass adopts, switching becomes prohibitively costly)
key_absences: Safety differential data (is one side empirically safer than the other?)
Transition case studies (Sweden 1967 Dagen H as natural experiment)

axes.structural_delta: Two equally functional equilibria exist; neither is inherently superior absent network effects
axes.primary_observable: Traffic flow efficiency metrics; accident rates controlling for other factors; no systematic advantage to either side in isolation
axes.selection_reason: Foundational mountain establishing the coordination game structure; feeds into both downstream axes

axes.human_readable: Network Effect Lock-In (Value Increases with Adoption)
axes.structural_delta: Each additional adopter increases the value of the convention for all existing adopters
axes.primary_observable: Cross-border traffic volume; vehicle import/export patterns; manufacturing economies of scale for right-hand-drive vs left-hand-drive vehicles
axes.selection_reason: Distinct observable (network value) from coordination structure; independent mechanism that amplifies lock-in

axes.structural_delta: Cost of changing convention includes infrastructure redesign, vehicle fleet replacement, retraining, and transition-period accident risk
axes.primary_observable: Sweden 1967 transition cost estimates; infrastructure replacement costs; accident rate spikes during transition periods
axes.selection_reason: Highest centrality; synthesis node where coordination structure and network effects create extractive barrier to optimization

axes.structural_delta: Current distribution reflects historical accidents (Napoleon's military campaigns, colonial inheritance) rather than functional optimization
axes.primary_observable: Geographic clustering of conventions correlating with historical political boundaries; former French colonies vs British colonies
axes.selection_reason: Distinct from coordination structure (explains distribution, not mechanism); piton documenting contingency rather than necessity

axes.structural_delta: Conflicting claims about whether right-hand or left-hand driving is safer, confounded by driver handedness and infrastructure quality
axes.primary_observable: Accident rate studies controlling for GDP, road quality, and enforcement; right-eye dominance vs right-hand dominance interaction effects
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: empirical uncertainty rather than structural constraint; if safety differential were established, would upgrade coordination_equilibrium_structure from mountain to rope

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Contested empirical claims about relative safety of right vs left
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Empirical uncertainty rather than structural constraint; outcome would reclassify coordination_equilibrium_structure if resolved

omegas.description: Is coordination_equilibrium_structure truly a mountain (no inherent advantage to either side) or does unresolved safety research reveal one side as objectively superior? If safety differential exists, the mountain becomes a rope of suboptimal coordination.

Does autonomous vehicle technology eliminate the coordination problem by allowing vehicles to adapt to local convention dynamically? If so, switching_cost_barrier collapses and network_effect_lock_in weakens.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory) - technological disruption not addressed in extraction

omegas.description: Are there regional contexts (island nations, isolated road networks) where switching costs are low enough that optimization becomes feasible? Samoa 2009 switch suggests boundary conditions on switching_cost_barrier.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) - small-scale transitions may reveal beneficiaries of standardization

fracture_scan.notes: F03 detected: coordination_equilibrium_structure classified as mountain (no inherent advantage to either side) but safety research remains contested and confounded. If empirical work establishes a safety differential, the mountain reclassifies as a rope of suboptimal coordination. Generated omega_mountain_validity to bound this uncertainty.
